You can use your own words to report other people's words and thoughts. There are many different reporting verbs that can help you express in your own words what people have said.
You have indicated that you are committed to doing this.

You can use some reporting verbs with or without an object after it and before the that-clause. Some verbs, however, require a preposition after the verb if an object is used. Different verbs need different prepositions. Let's look at verbs that need to, with and of when followed by an object.

To:
The actress said that she was very nervous about the award ceremony.
Margaret complained that she was very tired.
If you want to include a personal object before the that-clause:

The actress said to me that she was very nervous about the award ceremony.
Margaret complained to her husband that she was very tired.
Other verbs that use “to” include: say, admit, suggest, complain, point out, explain, announce, confess, recommend, report, indicate, propose and mention.

With:
You can use with .after agree, disagree, joke, check .and argue.
The woman argued with her husband that. the television was too loud.

Of:
In more formal situations, you use of with ask, require and demand.
The teacher asked (of her students) that they study hard.
The coach demanded (of his players) that they focus on the game.

More informally, you can simply use a to-infinitive clause with ask and require. It is impossible to use a to-infinitive clause with demand.
The teacher asked her students to study hard.
You promised us that we would do a dessert that we can eat during the cleanse.
You asked me to prove that you could have dessert without refined sugar and dairy.
You hinted that that was your favorite.
You said you wanted to help.
My friend John requested that I pass on some of the best recipes to him.
Unreal Conditional in the Present and Future - Review
You can talk about situations in the present and future that are not likely to happen or impossible. You use conditional sentences to do this.
If I could have something sweet every day this month, I would be very happy!
If you could choose any flavor to have, what would it be?
Should you need more ideas, there are hundreds of resources on the internet.
If you would just put aside your doubts for a while, I'll show you that dessert can be healthy.
If I could eat this at every meal, I would!

You can use a conditional sentence to talk about:
  • a present situation that is impossible (this sentence is the opposite of the truth)
  • a future situation that is unlikely to happen (you are imagining the future possibility, speaking hypothetically)
Structure:

If + simple past, … would + base form of the verb
If I had more free time, I would read more books.

would + base form of the verb ... if + simple past
I would read more books if I had more free time.

You can use other verbs instead of would + base form of the verb. You can use:
  • could (meaning: would be able to)
    If I were more flexible, I could be a gymnast.
  • might (meaning: it's possible, but unlikely)
    If I didn't smoke so much, I might have fewer breathing problems.

You can use if + would for polite requests:
If you would call me later, I would be less busy then.

You can use if + should to show that a situation is highly unlikely.
If you should see the manager, don't say anything about the angry customer.

You can also use by any chance in the same way:
If by any chance you see the manager, don't say anything about the angry customer.

More formally, begin the sentence with should:
Should you see the manager, don't say anything about the angry customer.
Go to restaurant of your choice and have a meal.
Take notes on the food as you are eating. Use adjectives to describe the flavor and quality of the meal.
Write a paragraph about the meal and the restaurant. Tell whether you would recommend the restaurant or not and why.
Exchange reviews with a partner. Would you like to go to the restaurant that your friend reviewed?
I describe a meal in a restaurant.
I write a paragraph about whether or not I would recommend the restaurant.
I read a partner's restaurant review and decide if I would go to the restaurant.

images.text:
Vanessa: So, we've made a couple healthy meals that will fit into your cleanse diet. You have lots of recipes to work with and you both have lots of creative ideas. I think you will be very successful and efficacious with this cleanse. You have indicated that you are committed to doing this. Should you need more ideas, there are hundreds of resources on the internet.
Amy: You promised us that we would do a dessert that we can eat during the cleanse. If I could have something sweet every day this month, I would be very happy!

Vanessa: Okay, let's find a dessert recipe and make it together. You asked me to prove that you could have dessert without refined sugar and dairy and I'm going to do it! If you could choose any flavor to have, what would it be?
Amy: Caramel.
Peter: You hinted that that was your favorite dessert. How about this? Sticky Toffee Pecan Pudding.
Amy: That sounds amazing! And look, no refined sugar or butter or eggs. How is it possible that this is dessert?

Vanessa: You'll see. If you would just put aside your doubts for a while, I'll show you that dessert can be healthy. Let's get cracking on the cake. Peter, you said you wanted to help so why don't you toast the pecans. I'll mix together the almond milk, dates and baking soda and Amy can whisk together the oil and honey.
Peter: My friend John requested that I pass on some of the best recipes to him. I think he'll like this one.
Vanessa: While the cake is baking, we can make the toffee sauce. Peter, whisk together those ingredients and heat them on the stove. You need to be attentive with this. Keep stirring and don't let it burn. Amy and I will sit here and chew the fat.
Peter: It smells so good! If I could eat this at every meal, I would!
